note: The standard reference on why clinical AI stalls between research and practice, still the clearest statement of the gap.
title: Key challenges for delivering clinical impact with artificial intelligence

reading.body:
Published in 2019, this remains the standard reference on why clinical AI stalls between research success and practical deployment, and it is still the clearest statement of that gap.

That a 2019 paper is still the standard reference, cited 2,906 times, suggests the specific gap it identified, between a model performing well on a research dataset and a model working reliably in actual clinical practice, has not been closed by the intervening years of model improvement. The 2024 clinical decision-making paper elsewhere in this collection, showing frontier models still diagnosing worse than physicians, is recent evidence that the gap this paper described persists.

The paper predates the current generation of large language models, so its specific technical recommendations should be read as historically foundational rather than current.

explain_beginner: This paper asks why so many impressive sounding results for AI in medicine, models that can supposedly spot cancer or eye disease as well as expert doctors, so rarely turn into something patients actually benefit from in a real hospital. It matters because by 2019 there was already a flood of papers claiming human level performance for medical AI, and this paper's authors, from a leading AI research lab's health division, wanted to explain the specific gap between a model doing well on a test dataset and that same model actually helping patients get better care. They found several concrete reasons for the gap, models trained on old data can quietly get worse as real world clinical practice shifts, models can accidentally learn to rely on irrelevant details in images rather than the medical signal itself, most studies never test whether the model works on patients and equipment from a different hospital than the one it was trained on, and many studies never even measure whether patients ended up healthier as a result. It does not offer a technical fix for these problems, it is a diagnosis of the field's shortcomings, and it stops short of predicting how quickly the field will actually close these gaps.
explain_business: For a hospital, health system, or health tech investor evaluating a diagnostic AI product, the single most actionable fact from this widely cited paper, now with well over a thousand citations, is the external validation statistic, only about 6 percent of published medical imaging AI studies tested performance outside the original training site, so a vendor's headline accuracy number should be treated as unproven for your specific patient population and equipment until validated locally. The ruler artifact example is a concrete illustration of a real procurement risk, a model can post excellent benchmark accuracy while actually keying off an irrelevant correlated detail rather than genuine medical signal, which only shows up once you test on your own different data. The INFANT trial example is the compliance relevant fact for anyone tempted to approve a tool based on accuracy alone, higher measured accuracy did not produce better patient outcomes in that real trial, meaning outcome data, not just accuracy scores, should be a contractual requirement before wider deployment. This applies now, in 2026, to essentially any clinical AI purchase, the specific fix the paper calls for, independent external validation and prospective outcome trials before rollout, remains the standard a buyer should insist on since these problems were structural to the field rather than specific to any one now outdated model.
explain_practitioner: Written as a narrative synthesis surveying dozens of existing studies of medical AI, the paper identifies specific and named failure modes rather than staying abstract. It documents dataset shift, where a model's performance degrades as clinical practice or patient populations change after training, and confounding, citing a memorable concrete example where an image classification algorithm partly relied on the presence of a ruler in dermatology photos, which correlated with malignant lesions being measured, rather than on the lesion itself. It reports that in a survey of 516 published medical imaging AI studies, only about 6 percent performed any external validation on data from outside the original training site, meaning the vast majority of published accuracy claims had not been tested against a genuinely independent population. It also cites a randomized clinical trial, the INFANT trial, as a cautionary case where a system with measurably higher diagnostic accuracy did not translate into better patient outcomes once deployed in an actual clinical trial, directly undercutting the assumption that better benchmark accuracy automatically means better care. The authors state plainly that most published evidence for medical AI comes from retrospective studies rather than prospective trials, and that algorithmic bias, including underperformance on darker skin tones in melanoma detection tools, remains inadequately measured across the field.
